question: What is the main focus of a National Drug Policy compared to a general health policy?

options.B: Medical doctor and nurse salary structures

explanation: Think of it this way: while a general health policy looks at everything in healthcare, a National Drug Policy zooms in specifically on medicines—making sure they are produced, distributed, and used safely!

question: Why must a National Drug Policy tie in closely with the National Health Policy?

options.A: It allows pharmaceutical companies to set their own market prices without government interference.
options.B: International donors will refuse to release funds if the two policies are separate documents.
options.C: Medications are essential therapeutic tools required to achieve overall population health goals.
options.D: It prevents nurses from having to purchase hospital supplies out of their own pockets.

explanation: You can't achieve a healthy nation without medicines! Because drugs are our most common tool for treatment, the drug policy has to support the country's bigger health goals.

question: When did Nigeria introduce its first official National Drug Policy to fix chaotic drug distribution?
explanation: Nigeria rolled out its very first formal National Drug Policy back in 1990 to clean up unregulated drug imports and fight fake medicines.

question: What major problem pushed Nigeria to create its early drug policies?

options.A: A mandate from private pharmaceutical companies to raise drug prices
options.B: The widespread circulation of fake and adulterated drugs in open markets
options.C: The sudden surplus of locally manufactured vaccines and antibiotics
options.D: The complete absence of hospitals and clinics in rural communities

explanation: Open drug markets were flooded with fake and harmful products. This huge public health danger forced the government to step in with strict rules.

question: Which of these is a core pillar of the National Drug Policy?

options.B: Quality, safety, and efficacy of medicines
options.C: Privatization of all public teaching hospitals
options.D: Elimination of nursing schools in rural areas

explanation: Spot on! Making sure drugs are safe, work properly (efficacy), and are top quality is the heart of any good drug policy.

question: A clinic administrator is buying medications following the National Drug Policy. What should guide this choice?

options.A: Purchasing large quantities of single-use antibiotics regardless of disease patterns
options.B: Focusing on safety, efficacy, affordability, and availability of essential medicines
options.C: Stocking only medications that are heavily advertised on television and radio
options.D: Buying the most expensive imported brands to guarantee maximum patient prestige

explanation: When stocking a clinic, we always look for drugs that are safe, work well, patients can afford, and are actually available when needed!

question: Which agency is primarily responsible for regulating drugs in Nigeria?
explanation: NAFDAC is our frontline agency charged with checking and controlling food, drugs, cosmetics, and medical devices across Nigeria.

question: Why must a nurse check for an official agency registration number on a drug before giving it?

options.A: To determine which pharmaceutical company manufactured the raw chemical compound
options.B: To calculate the exact wholesale profit margin for the hospital pharmacy
options.C: To ensure the medication qualifies for international shipping exemptions
options.D: To confirm that the drug has been evaluated for safety, quality, and efficacy

explanation: That registration number is your safety green light! It tells you NFDAC or the relevant body has tested the drug and approved it for use.

question: What is the main idea behind the Essential Medicines Concept?

options.A: The mandatory use of expensive imported brand-name drugs over generics
options.B: A select list of priority drugs that meet the healthcare needs of the majority
options.C: Stocking every single pharmaceutical formulation ever invented in every clinic
options.D: Allowing patients to dispense their own prescription drugs without guidance

explanation: Essential medicines are a carefully picked list of priority drugs that treat the most common health needs of everyday people effectively and cheaply.

question: Which of these clinical actions goes against the rules of rational drug use?

options.A: Prescribing strong broad-spectrum antibiotics for a simple viral upper respiratory infection
options.B: Educating a diabetic patient on the correct technique for self-administering insulin
options.C: Administering a standard dose of paracetamol for a documented fever in an adult
options.D: Checking a patient's kidney function before starting a new maintenance medication

explanation: Remember: antibiotics fight bacteria, not viruses! Giving them for a simple cold or viral infection wastes medicine and causes drug resistance.

question: What is the difference between substandard and counterfeit medications?

options.A: Substandard drugs are manufactured locally, while counterfeit drugs are always imported.
options.B: Counterfeit drugs are cheaper versions of safe generics produced by licensed companies.
options.C: Substandard drugs fail quality specifications, while counterfeit drugs are deliberately mislabeled copies.
options.D: Substandard drugs have expired dates, while counterfeit drugs contain too much active ingredient.

explanation: Substandard drugs are usually genuine products that missed quality marks, while counterfeits are fake, fraudulent copies made to deceive us.

question: A patient with severe malaria isn't getting better despite finishing a full course of drugs bought from an unverified roadside vendor. What should you suspect?

options.A: The patient requires an immediate surgical intervention for appendicitis.
options.B: The hospital ward is experiencing an outbreak of a normal bacterial infection.
options.C: The patient's body has suddenly developed a lifelong immunity to all fevers.
options.D: The medication administered may be substandard or counterfeit.

explanation: When a trusted drug completely fails to work—especially from a shady source—always suspect that it might be a fake or low-quality product.

question: What is a key way nurses support national drug policies right at the bedside?

options.A: Manufacturing basic intravenous fluids in the hospital ward kitchen
options.B: Monitoring patient responses and reporting adverse drug reactions
options.C: Issuing official manufacturing licenses to private pharmaceutical companies
options.D: Setting market retail prices for all imported prescription drugs

explanation: As bedside nurses, we watch patients closely after giving medications. Spotting and reporting side effects or bad reactions helps keep drug safety in check!

question: Why is the nurse's role so crucial for making a National Drug Policy work in real life?

options.A: Nurses are solely responsible for importing essential medicines from international manufacturers.
options.B: Nurses are the frontline professionals who handle, administer, and educate patients about medications daily.
options.C: Nurses hold the legal authority to shut down illegal open-air drug markets across the country.
options.D: Nurses write the legal statutes that govern pharmaceutical practice in government courts.

explanation: Policies are just paper until we put them into practice! Because nurses handle, give, and teach about drugs every day, our actions make the policy a success.
